correctness.rationale: For fixed 4s observations, finite fourth moments uniformly control all squared-distance fluctuations at O_p(sqrt d). A common possibly random bandwidth scaled to c*d yields a pairwise RBF Taylor expansion with O_p(1/d) uniform remainder. After first-half evaluation, the random norm difference is exactly common to all scores and cancels in numerator and group-centered variances. The multivariate coordinate CLT makes the 2s projected first-half scores iid Gaussian with variance 2 sigma^4/s, leading to the exact pooled t ratio scaled sqrt(s/(s-1)). Continuous mapping applies because the chi-square denominator is nonzero almost surely. Reproduced numerical implementation tests corroborate the formula but are not the proof.

originality.rationale: Best-knowledge comparison with the original NeurIPS xMMD and its expanded open-access preprint, separate unsplit high-dimensional MMD, held-out WiTS, targeted public literature, related mathematical records, and accessible owned findings reveals no direct fixed-s, dimension-only Student null theorem for characteristic RBF cross-MMD. Normality theorems with sample sizes increasing do not imply the fixed-s limit; exact classical Student algebra alone does not establish the kernel-to-Gaussian projection step. Priority uncertainty is explicitly retained.
residual_risks: Earlier unindexed or non-open-access general fixed-test-sample kernel witness theorem may imply the result.
Related 2023 high-dimensional unsplit MMD full appendices were not read entirely, but the explicitly different statistic and joint-growth premise make direct coverage unlikely.
Review is not an independent originality certification.

value.rationale: Identifies a substantive, quantitatively large null-size failure of the Gaussian cutoff in the fixed-sample high-dimensional regime for a published permutation-free characteristic-kernel test. At four observations per group, the limiting nominal 5% size is about 18.24%; the exact scaled-Student critical value remedies the identified mismatch. The theorem treats the usual median-bandwidth scale and arbitrary finite-fourth-moment independent coordinate laws, showing structural rather than isolated numerical behavior.
